utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there was one preliminary matter to be raised by the Prosecution. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, good morning. Just to respond to and accept the Chamber's invitation at the end of the hearing Thursday to put our requests for admission regarding portions of Mr. Basara's previous statements on the record. The Prosecution asks that 65 ter 27968a, an excerpt from a record of Basara's prior recorded interview, be admitted as P7322 which number has been reserved for an excerpt from that interview. The Prosecution also tenders 65 ter 31876a, an excerpt from Mr. Basara's testimony in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know what's the proper should be then, asked to include what we want from those transcripts and interviews?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to add anything, of course then the question arises to what extent the portions you are seeking, whether they have been dealt with by the witness. I mean, it's not just an extract coming out of the blue, but of course it's because attention has been paid or at least the matter has been covered. But if you want to think about that. Mr. Traldi, I take it that you'll give Mr. Lukic sufficient time to consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. President. And I've just been reminded that the specific pages that we used and the transcript pages on which those pages of his previous interview and testimony were used during his examination are provided in an e-mail we sent to the Chambers and Defence on 24 April at 10.44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I take it that you want to review and see what your response will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll wait for a while, but we now know what is uploaded in order to be -- at this moment what is uploaded where the Prosecution seeks 7322 admission and also what is uploaded as well as the extracts from the testimony is concerned. Would it be wise to have already a number reserved for that as well? Mr. Registrar, for 31876a could you provisionally assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P7389, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7389 is reserved for that purpose. Mr. Lukic, we'll hear from you, well, let's say, this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we postpone it till the next week? This week is really full for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the next week means a postponement of four weeks, but if you do it by e-mail then -- this is indeed a very full week, so if it is -- well, let's say this month still. And if it's not this week, then you can do it by -- through e-mail.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we'll see after that. Is the -- is the Defence ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. Mr. Savo Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. But perhaps before the witness enters the courtroom, Mr. Registrar, I'd like to briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know where ... could someone check whether the witness is waiting behind the doors or still on its way?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If you don't mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness should be on his way. I would not have minded at all, I would have appreciated it, but I see the door is opening already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I spoke too quickly because my appreciation, Mr. Traldi, disappeared from the transcript, which it should not. Good morning, Mr. Sokanovic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you. Good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sokanovic. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, be seated. Mr. Sokanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: We speak the same language, so I will make sure to pause after your answers, and you try to do the same after my questions. This is for the benefit of the interpreters who need to interpret everything. Could you please slowly tell us your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Savo Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your father's name, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Maj father's name was Vojislav. I was born on the 27th January 1951 in Malo Polje hamlet near Kozlovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Your municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: General, could you just briefly tell us something about your education. Which schools did you finish?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I finished the elementary school in the place where I was born. After that, I completed the air force high school, the air high school for politics of the JNA, the school of politics, and the school of national defence after the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: When you attended Military Academy, what were you studying? I believe that it was not recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I specialised in telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Again, I believe that your answer is not complete. Telecommunications in what field?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Air force and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now could you please give us the time-frame as much as can you remember of your professional career. Where did you serve and what positions did you occupy before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I completed a Military Academy in 1973. Up to 1978, I worked as the commander of the independent platoon of communications battalion in Sarajevo. It was 321st Platoon. From 1978 until 1992, i.e., when the war broke out in the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I performed various duties in the educational centre of the air force and anti-aircraft defence in Rajlovac in Sarajevo. I was the commander of the cadet platoon. I was a teacher, assistant commander of the cadet battalion. I was in charge of a group of teachers, assistant commander of the secondary military school for air force and anti-aircraft defence. Then I was a teacher at Military Academy for -- of air force and anti-aircraft defence. I was the head of -- of -- an educational programme. And finally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the last position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your last position. The interpreters could not follow you.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander of the Military Academy of air force and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, where were you and did you stay there or were you assigned to a different duty?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, my belief, and I believe that that belief was shared by most of my colleagues, was that Bosnia-Herzegovina as a multi-ethnic state is not a place where a war could ever happen. However, as the conflict spread from Slavonia across Croatia, and it could already be felt in the air that it would spread onto Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, certain members of the cadet contingent and members of the faculty started leaving the JNA and moving back to their own midst. At the same time, information started reaching us, despite our belief that there would be no conflict, that various paramilitary formations were being set up, such as the Green Berets and the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question, Mr. Lukic, had been where were you when the war started. We haven't got an answer to that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will go back to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: You have just heard the Judge's intervention.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was teaching at the Military Academy of air force and anti-aircraft defence. When the war broke out, for a while, I was at Butmir airport together with some of the cadets and teachers from the academy.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Why did you go to Butmir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: We received a task from our commander, actually the commander of the 2nd Military District, to protect the infrastructure at the airport, the facilities there, and the equipment that was stored there.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: When you finished work, did you go home? How did you move about at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't go home. Not only then but even before then. For at least a month or two months we would go home only occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Because conflicts had already started, interethnic conflicts, and the JNA and the 2nd Military District tried to prevent interethnic conflicts. And we were on duty all the time, and those of us who had to be engaged were engaged. Not me personally. At the time, I was not engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Where does your family live in the spring 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of April, they lived in Sarajevo. And then they fled, became refugees, I don't know how to express it, or they were expelled first to Bijeljina and then to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you when the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, 1992, with the last remnants of the Military Academy, I transferred from Butmir airport to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the end of July, I believe it was the 31st of July, I returned and joined the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you assigned? Where were you deployed in the end of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I reported to the Main Staff, and I was assigned to the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: How many people were you in that sector; if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived, there were seven members in that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: To what level were you manned in that sector?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to have 40 men, and we were eight.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: While we're on the subject, what were the main problems in the organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There were many problems. A state of war had not been declared so that the army operated and worked under peacetime laws; whereas, in practice, it was in war already. That made command very difficult but also all the other activities and responsibilities of the commands. Second, the army did not have a centralised and unified system of procurement and equipment. It lacked all the necessary elements. It had to rely primarily on local communities and businesses on the ground. Third, in the organisation of the army, there were two prevailing concepts: One concept that supported the establishment of units, primarily brigades, based on the territorial principle; and the second concept advocating that the army should be organised based on ex-territorial manning, and that second principle was backed by the Main Staff. Another problem for the army was the lack of the necessary unified and uniform care for the families of fallen fighters and the population that had left its own areas of residence, so many of our personnel were preoccupied with their own family problems, including members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To what level were you manned with professional officers?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: To a very small extent. The manning level was very low.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some numbers.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Relative to the total number of personnel in the army, the percentage of professional officers was 2 to 3 per cent, at a maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: And the territory that you were supposed to defend? What was it like?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The territory was very stretched out with a very long line of separation with the opposing sides, upward of 2.000 kilometres which made it impossible to employ the army adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to your own sector. Did your sector have smaller organisational units; and, if so, what kind?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Our sector was organised into sections, and there were four sections: The section for morale and religious affairs; the section for information; the section for civilian affairs; and the section for legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: In which section were you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was deployed in the section for morale and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: You've told us earlier that the manning level was not good in your entire sector. Was there a section that didn't have a single member?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The section for civilian affairs had nobody. In one part of the section for morale and religious affairs, in addition to two persons who were dealing with morale and morale guidance, the same people had to deal with religious affairs, because there was nobody specialising in that. And in the section for information, there were two people; and in the section for legal affairs also two.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: In the section for information, who was working there? What was their rank?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, the head of section was Sergeant Borislav Djurdjevic, a staff-sergeant, and there was another person who was a typist. Later, heads of sections rotated. For a while, it was Captain First Class Mladen Petrovic. Then for two months, it was Colonel Vukota Vukovic. Then for a longer while, it was Colonel Stanko Misic. And in the end, Colonel Milovan Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: General Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: And who was superior to General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your position in the sector?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was head of the section for morale, guidance and religious affairs. In the beginning, my rank was lieutenant-colonel and then I was promoted into colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of the war, did you become head of one of the sections or sectors? Did you change position during the war?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No. The answers to both questions is no.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: When did you become head of section for moral guidance?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In December 1992. Until then, I was a desk officer in the section.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: During the war, were you reassigned to any other duties?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: In your sector for morale guidance, religious, legal affairs, did sections regularly meet?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: When would they meet, if ever?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Between sections, communication was usually through direct contact and by telephone. Because part of the sector was deployed at the main command post in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another part was in Han Pijesak, and communication was then usually by phone, especially during cease-fires, then we would meet all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you said that you had contacts by telephone because part of the sector was deployed at the main command post in ... And then the interpreters did not hear where that main command post was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the main command post deployed in Crna Rijeka, and another part was in the logistical command post in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the main command post.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: How did the reporting go inside the sector and vis-à-vis the rest of the Main Staff and who reported to the Main Staff on issues of moral guidance, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Heads of sections usually reported by telephone to the superior - that is to say, head of the sector - except for me who was there, so I did not need to use the telephone so often. The head of sector, I suppose, reported to the Main Staff - that is to say, the commander and assistant commanders - at occasional meetings or in direct contact, especially in situations when something important from the area of our sector was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Did units report on these issues to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: On issues concerning moral guidance and other issues relevant to our sector, subordinate units made monthly reports and submitted them to the Main Staff, and in the Main Staff it would be put on the desk of the head of sector and then forwarded to me or somebody else from the sector itself. In addition to that, if there was an event relevant and important for morale between two reports, subordinate units would send an interim report, but that happened rarely. And, finally, as part of the regular daily combat reports, there was an item dedicated to the level of morale and the situation on our territory, on the territory of the unit. And that part of the report was written by organs in the command who were in charge of reports, and the head of sector at the Main Staff had the responsibility to look at that part of the combat report or, if he was absent, then I would do it.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you just explain the competencies and the main tasks of the sector for morale guidance, religious and legal affairs, and your main responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The section for morale guidance and religious affairs --

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, just a moment. I believe that my question did not have to do with the sector primarily. It is not correctly recorded. I'll repeat it. Could you explain the competencies and the principle tasks of the section for morale guidance within the sector for morale guidance, religious and legal affairs, and your main responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Section for morale guidance monitored the state of morale and factors that had a positive impact on the troops' morale and those who had a negative impact on the troops' morale. Based on instructions -- or rather, the instruction for monitoring and assessing combat morale in the Army of Republika Srpska which was issued in 1992, the section used the indicators from the instruction to assess combat morale. All that was done based on the monthly reports received from subordinated units, based on the information contained in regular daily reports, based on the information personally gathered by the officers who visited the units or any other information. Based on all that, the section compiled its reports on the troops' morale for the previous month. All the elements were incorporated, and there was also a conclusion and the proposal of measures that had to be undertaken at the level of subordinated units and commands. There was also a proposal for the contents of those measures that would be undertaken by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska itself. There was also a proposal of the measures that should be undertaken by the Supreme Command, i.e., the highest state organs, all with a view to strengthening the troops' morale. That information was sent to the commanders' collegium and, more often than that, because not everybody was present at those meetings, the information of that nature was looked at by the chief of sector, and all those who participated would make their proposals. The report was fine-tuned and sent to the president of the republic. And the subordinated the units were sent this for their information only, and feedback was requested from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the Chamber has now listened for some 45 minutes to matters of which most of them at least they do escape our sense of relevance. Try to get to the points you want to make with this witness, because if you want to counter the evidence presented by the Prosecution, which is, of course, also including structures but always in one way or another related to the crimes charged, get to a point that we understand how the evidence of this witness challenges the evidence presented by the Prosecution, rather than in vague terms as: To this was the organisation sometimes people attended; sometimes people did not attend. We had meetings, but sometimes we had no meetings. Get to the point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it does take -- when it's live testimony, it does take to have some introduction, and I think that it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, fine. I understand that. That's the reason why I'm saying that 80 per cent of the testimony escapes our relevance. Some introduction, fine. We now -- you've scheduled it for two and a half hours. We have listened 45 minutes to introduction. Get to what you want to convince the Chamber of. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have P5082 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, we have a tight schedule this week, so we're not very much inclined if examination proceeds as it does now to grant any additional time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this document was drafted in February 1995, and it is about the responsibilities and the recruitment of the organ for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs in the units and institutions of the Army of Republika Srpska. At the end of the document, on the last page thereof, there is a typed name of General Ratko Mladic. In the version that we have, there is no signature; however, in the document on the screen, we see that there is a signature, as a matter of fact. Can I go back to the first page, please. Thank you. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this document have anything to do with your division or your sector?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This is about the responsibilities and the recruitment of the organ for moral guidance, religious, and legal affairs in the Army of Republika, the entire army. The document was drafted by the sector. Chiefs of various decisions used the rules and their experience to work out those responsibilities. So this document covers the entire military ranging from the General Staff to the lowest of units, i.e., a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about the relationship with the media. What was the position of the Main Staff and your division and sector vis-à-vis the media, both national and foreign, and representatives of international organisations?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That was within the purview of the division for information. The attitude towards international -- or, rather, the relationship with UNPROFOR and other international organisations was within the purview of the division for co-operation with international organisations. To be very concrete and answer your question, the position was that we should be fair and professional in dealing with journalists and representatives of international organisations. The same was requested from them; i.e., there should have been reciprocity in our mutual relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D5391.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was issued on the 15th of March, 1995. The document was signed, and we don't need to see it, or, rather, it was signed on behalf of General Milan Gvero. Since this is a teletyped message, the signature is not displayed. It was sent to all the corps, as you can see, and to some other addressees to some other units. In the first paragraph, we read: "We have lately been aware that commands and units are following different procedures in informing the public and treating domestic and foreign journalists whereby they are seriously violating the guide-lines on informing the public about the VRS, order of the RS president ... issued in 1994 and other orders regulating these issues. Such behaviour has resulted in revealing an increased amount of information constituting military secrets, which...." First of all, you've seen this document during proofing. How come that military secrets were leaked? What was the procedure when it came to keeping military secrets?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Disclosing confidential military information which primarily concerned the deployment, the size, the strength, the equipment, the planned tasks, results, this information was leaked in two ways. The first one was -- originated from the units. Desk officers or assistant commanders for moral guidance and information were poorly informed and for other reasons leaked information that constituted revealing military secrets. And the second case was when journalists visited the deployment area of a unit, sometime with the best of intent and sometimes not, published information that constituted revealing military secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the role of the sector headed by General Gvero when it came to the protection of military secrets?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, i.e., 1992, the sector issued an instruction on how to inform the general public about the activities of the VRS, and this instruction is referred to in this document as well. Later on, on several occasions whenever certain occurrences were observed, it issued additional instructions. The chief of sector's personal attitude was that these instructions had to be strictly observed, that military intelligence had to be kept secret because there were occasions when a leakage of such confidential information cost lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear your last words.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this document into evidence, 1D05391.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1053, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. We're close to a break, Mr. Lukic. Still, even that military secrets should be kept confidential, should not leak, is not an astonishing thing, and the link to the crimes charged is still not clear to us, and therefore also not the relevance of this information. And that's for the last well over ten minutes now that we have listened to that. I mean, if there would have been no leakage, would that have changed considerably the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman is in the sector of morale and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But it's about relevance for this case; that's what I'm talking about. I leave it to that. You have two minutes until the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 14781, please.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this is a document which was issued on the 20th of June, 1992. Its title is: "Prevention of Reprisal and Treatment of Journalists and Representatives of International Organisations." Under 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's the break time. Maybe we should first go to the break and return, because this one will probably take another five to ten minutes for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'll take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I would briefly like to deal with P1655. The Prosecution has requested on the 5th of May during the testimony of Nedjelko Trkulja that Exhibit P1655 not be broadcast. The exhibit was then temporarily placed under seal and the Chamber requests that the Prosecution provide further information on the record this week as to why Exhibit P1655 should be kept confidential. Of course, we do not know whether that needs to be done confidentially or not, but I leave that in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we have before us a document dated 20th June, 1992, a document from the Main Staff of the VRS. As we see at the bottom, the name of Major-General Milan Gvero is typewritten. Let me just ask you: What was the position, the policy of the Main Staff, towards the civilian population of the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff did not treat any civilian population as its adversary or enemy that should be attacked. On the contrary, the position was that the civilian population should be treated properly, correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the Main Staff, through its subordinate units, try to organise expulsions of that population, torching and looting of their property?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: If information reached the Main Staff about such actions, such as torching of property or any action against civilians, what would the Main Staff do?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As we see from this document of the sector, the persons involved were cautioned and instructions were issued as to what should be done and what consequences would be triggered by failure to obey, and the security organs initiated, or at least should initiate, criminal complaints if such things happened. I can give you one example. The Main Staff itself was located less than 1 kilometre from a Muslim settlement, and for a very long time no measures were taken, although there had been incidents created by the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm then wondering how the answer continues. What then happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you are giving an example of what was done if anyone from your armed force would do anything against civilian population. You give an example but you said: For very long time, no measures were taken although there had been incidents created by the other side. So apparently are you talking about not protecting the civilian population again actions undertaken by your own soldiers but by the others. Could you give us one example of ill-treatment of the civilian population reported and then what action was taken against your own soldiers that had shown this behaviour against the civilian population? Just one example to start with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe what I said was not interpreted properly or maybe I was not clear enough. I cited an example where the civilian population very close to the Main Staff, less than 1 kilometre, lived and enjoyed protection from our side. Anyone who wanted to do anything against that civilian population was stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the kind of example I'm seeking. What I'd like you to tell us of one instance where your own soldiers misbehaved against the civilian population and what action was then taken in terms of investigations, prosecutions, whatever. Could you give us one such example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot give you an example like that because I can't remember. That was within the purview of the prosecutor's offices and the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you're telling us that whenever this was reported, action would be taken, et cetera, et cetera, so apparently you are familiar with what should have been but -- and I think it touches upon the morale as well, and you show us this document. But not one example of your own soldiers misbehaving and then action taken by the Main Staff to investigate or to prosecute or whatever. No example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. And this is exactly the difference between general observations and concrete facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is exactly why we introduced that long introduction, to show you what competencies of this gentlemen were [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But finally to -- [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At last, I will follow your questions now trying further to clarify what his role was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I am and this Chamber is very much interested, I'm not saying exclusively, but very much interested in what happened on the ground. And now we've seen a document which states what should be done, and then my question is was that done, and then the witness can't give us any example, so we are remaining then very much on the abstract level; whereas, the Chamber is as much interested in the concrete level as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: General Sokanovic, your sector and your section, did they deal with investigations of criminal acts?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, and it was not in their area of work.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the role of your section in terms of preventative action?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Through our briefings, contacts, and in other ways, we cautioned about possible consequences of wrong-doing, but the fact that we cautioned doesn't mean that we were supposed to enforce it. The competent authorities were supposed to enforce it. Within the sector, our section, and within the Main Staff of the VRS, instructions applied to all the institutions and all the commands of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document signed by late Major-General -- or, rather, General Milan Gvero, we read: "In our previous documents, we have several times pointed out the need to prevent reprisals against innocent people (looting, burning, destruction, and maltreatment). "Such actions are not and must not be characteristic of the members of our army ..." These warnings addressed to subordinate units, were they honest and sincere in your opinion, or were they designed to conceal different behaviour that was pre-planned?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, these warnings were sincere.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: We discussed representatives of the foreign media. Were they in any kind of danger of reprisal?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Some people and a number of fighting men were wounded or killed, and their families, comrades in arms, and relatives were very embittered for that. I don't know for what reasons. Perhaps because of their pain and their experience. But they were in real danger of reprisal, and we also warned about that, and we pointed out the need to protect them from anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand the answer, Mr. Lukic. Your question was: Whether foreign media representatives were in any kind of danger. The witness says: "Some people and a number of fighting men were wounded ..." And he's talking about these fighting men being protected against danger. Now, would representatives of the foreign media be fighting people?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the dilemma voiced by Judge Moloto. Could you please explain what you meant.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: A number of fighting men but not only fighting men; also the civilian population were embittered and were hard-hit by the death of their comrades in arms or relatives or by their wounding. We thought it was possible when representatives of the foreign media appear, but not only the foreign media, also the local media, that could lead to embitterness -- bitterness, revolt, and even reprisal. I don't remember that a single foreign reporter was killed in the territory controlled by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of danger were foreign reporters in?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were at risk of being attacked or even liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from the warnings sent out by your sector, did you also provide security or was security the job of someone else?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean foreign reporters?

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Providing security to reporters in the territory of Republika Srpska, regardless of whether it was a combat zone or somewhere behind the lines was the responsibility of two types of authorities: Partly the Ministry of Interior and partly the army, especially when reporters would go to military installations or areas involved in the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Traldi or Mr. Tieger: Is endangering foreign journalists part of your case? Putting them at risk, attacking them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence of foreign journalists, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think you can see by the length of the discussion between Mr. Traldi and myself that we're hard-pressed to understand the precise relevance of this concern about journalists to the actual charges in the case. We're not suggesting that there isn't some manner in which it can bare on that, but as the Court's question itself suggested, it's not a specific charge and it's not particularly embedded in -- in the overall Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if there's no real issue about protecting foreign journalists to -- why do we hear that? --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sovanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's Mr. Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sokanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Second time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't correct you if you're speaking your own language, Mr. Lukic, but we also have to protect the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise to Mr. Sokanovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sokanovic, what was the position of the Main Staff? Were journalists to be allowed to write freely on what they wanted to see, obviously with the caveat from military secrets had to be protected? Were foreign journalists allowed to travel the length and the breadth of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The position of the Main Staff was to allow journalists to write freely, that they had to make sure that military secrets were not revealed, and that they could move freely wherever their own personal safety or military secrets were not threatened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, again a sweeping statement. We have heard detailed evidence about the first visit to Omarska by one of the journalists. We have seen quite a lot of documents about what happened in the Srebrenica area on details on who would be allowed yes or no. These sweeping statements do really not assist in better understanding the situation apart from -- I mean, these are but -- and we have seen that before, and we have heard other witnesses say in general every journalist was free to report and to go wherever he went unless, and of course the focus is on the "unless." Let's proceed. If the witness has any specific knowledge, specific events, specific limitations, in the freedom of movement of journalists and further reasons for that, we'd like to hear it very much, but general statements we've heard quite a bit. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are very impatient today, Your Honour. We'll come -- next document will speak about that. We will offer this one into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 14781 will be Exhibit D1054.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next document we would like to see 65 ter 05852.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sokanovic, the document before us was issued on the 26th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can see the bottom of the document in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document has a signature stamp of the deputy chief of sector, Colonel Savo Sokanovic. Is that you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your role in the Main Staff with regard to foreign journalists and reporters?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I expand on that, please? Not only foreign reporters but all reporters who wanted travel through Republika Srpska and visit certain facilities and units addressed the Ministry of Information of the government of Republika Srpska. More often than not they would present themselves personally at its door, and then that request was forwarded to the Department for Information which was in Han Pijesak. Since they didn't know what was the situation like in the field, whether there were any combat activities where the journalists wanted to go, they would forward that request to the chief of sector, i.e., myself, with a request to collect information and send the request back so that they could answer. That was a standard procedure that was applied. And then based on the position of the operative organ who was familiar with the situation on the field, the superior organs of information and security and its -- and their opinion, a consent or approval would be given for the journalists' free passage, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document, we can see that the team of ZDF journalists were allowed passage from Pale across Rogatica, Visegrad, towards Belgrade. Was all this information on combat activities also collected even when a team of journalists wanted to pass through? What was your role in the collection of that information?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As I've just explained, an approval was sought for every situation for a mere passage or a longer stay with a unit in an area of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: In your answer, you said what should have been done. Did you personally collect information, for example, from the security sector or from the operations sector in the area where combat was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was either me or one of the colleagues who were members of the organ at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: You have previously told us that the protection of those reporters was dual. We can see that they would be accompanied by the police patrols from Pale. How did you know that the MUP would be in charge of their security?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In two ways: One way was that part of the request was also police protection, which was then regulated in keeping with the rules of the Ministry of Interior; and the second way was when such teams passed through areas where there was no combat, so the military did not have to provide security. A previous order of the president of Republika Srpska defined that both the MUP and the military provided protection for teams of journalists as needed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be instructed to move away from the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you move slightly away from the microphone. Although I'm not certain that it -- this resonance is caused by the closeness or whether it's anything else. Could you please -- the usher will stay with you until after you have restarted answer -- started the answer to your next question. Mr. Lukic, security for journalists, as we established a minute ago, was not a major issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1055, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to ask you about humanitarian convoys. What do you know by the co-ordination body of the government of Republika Srpska that dealt with issues relative to humanitarian convoys?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Republika Srpska issued an order to set up a co-ordination body for humanitarian organisations. A representative of the military was a member of that body. That body was headed by Mr. Kalinic or Krajisnik, I'm not sure, somebody from the top echelons of the government. There was a member from the Ministry of the Interior. Another member was from the commissariat for refugees and displaced person. Humanitarian organisations that wanted to deliver humanitarian aid or do other things in the territory of Republika Srpska or those who wanted to pass through the territory of Republika Srpska had to address that co-ordination body. The representative of the military of Republika Srpska participated in the work of the co-ordination body and the final position of the co-ordination body was binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we 65 ter number 12957.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have just talked about this. This document was issued in December 1993, and it deals with the co-ordination body. You've already told us something about that. If the co-ordination body allowed a convoy to pass through the territory, what was the role of the military following such a decision?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Either the military or the police, depending on the nature of the convoy, if such a convoy just passed through Republika Srpska to go elsewhere, the military and the police were duty-bound to check the list of personnel and cargo of the convoy, and if there were no discrepancies or hindrances, they were supposed to allow their free and unhindered passage. If there was a problem, the convoy would be kept and the issue would be dealt in an adequate way. For example, sometimes they would enter with a surplus of cargo that was not covered by the convoy manifest. Such cargo would be kept at the check-point, and when the convoy returned on its way back it would pick up the cargo and take it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1056, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No speaking aloud, please. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. Yes, I first should have -- admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The record is not entirely clear. D1056 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to your sector, did it try to act pre-emptively with regard to POW camps?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did it in the following sense. Although this was not within the sector's jurisdiction, still we issued warnings about the respect for the rights of prisoners. We also stated that the representatives of the International Red Cross and other international organisations should be allowed free visits. So those were the warnings and instructions we issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any concrete example of such a warning, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens, Your Honour, 1D05432.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's an example, then there's no need for the witness to answer my question at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that there's no translation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of all the others who don't understand B/C/S, I will say that the document was issued on the 28th of May, 1993. The title is: "Instruction on the Actions of the Units of the Army of Republika Srpska when Visiting POW Camps and Military Investigation Prisons." On the last page, that is to say this next page, let's look at the signature. It's signed General Milan Gvero. And we see it was delivered to all the corps and the command of the air force and anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not signed, but the author is -- well, Mr. Lukic, sometimes you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you have commented on the situation. I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you accept that this was sent by Mr. Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke with this witness on this document during the preparation, and then I can ask him. It may be better then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking for the position of the Defence, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is -- it's typewritten. Whether he signed it or not, it cannot be seen from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is whether you accept that it was sent by Mr. Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is definitely not sent by Mr. Gvero. It's somebody from the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, that it was sent and that this was authored by General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can ask the witness. I cannot testify on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can -- you can present the position of the Defence on it, which may save a lot of questions as well now and then. But if you don't want to answer that question, then just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just if it might assist, we've got a translated version of what we believe to be the same document under a different ERN. It's uploaded under 65 ter 32561, and my colleague has just released it, in case Mr. Lukic would prefer to work with that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would certainly prefer to see the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have then 65 ter 32561, please. I can read this translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine that you can. First of all, you accept that it's the same -- it's not the same document but it's another copy of --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The same number appears on the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that's -- although it may be -- there were some -- some handwriting on it, but the typed text or the printed text is the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sokanovic, is this a document drafted in your sector?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Sometimes I speak too fast. Did this document originate in your sector; if you know?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We see the registry number from our sector. We can't see the signature because it was sent by teletype. A teletype cannot transmit a signature, but we see the stamp at the end confirming that a certain unit had received this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the second page of this document? We don't know if there is a stamp on this one. There is. It's slightly different stamp, but we -- we can use this document.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your sector, were you able to monitor the enforcement of this or is this just an instruction? Who was supposed to do something about this?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is only an instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was supposed to monitor its enforcement?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: POW prisons were established by corps, and each corps had a commander of such a prison. He was supposed to monitor the situation and report to the corps commander, and if the corps commander decided something was important enough, he would submit it to the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this document into evidence; so it's 65 ter 32561.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1057, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sokanovic, which service in the Main Staff was in charge of following the media?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the section for information within the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: At the Main Staff, were you able to follow foreign media such as the CNN, BBC, Deutsche Welle?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, was there any cable television in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about Bosnia-Herzegovina, but not where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have Internet?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you read foreign newspapers and did you receive foreign press?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: At the Main Staff, did you have satellite aerials to receive foreign TV programming?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now ask you about problems in getting information. In those years of war, were there any problems in gathering information?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was not head of that section, but I know for a fact that there were problems. I can even tell you about some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The first part of the problem was in gathering information. That is to say, whether the units from bottom to top regularly gather information and forward it to higher levels. That was the job of this section. But unfortunately, it was not the case. Due to lack of personnel or lack of experience, it functioned more or less in some places not at all, in other places moderately well. The second part of the problem was the lack of equipment. Cameras, printers, copying machines, communications equipment. It was very difficult to pass information on. The next problem was with generalisations. Inadequately trained people were not always able to make an appropriate analysis and summarise information into reports. Communication was towards units and towards the public. There were limitations to our technical ability. As far as the operation of the army is concerned, a particular problem was that our troops were stretched thin along an extremely long separation line. It was not always possible for troops on the front line to be well-informed unless a company commander would go from trench to trench and inform them personally because he was unable to gather them for a briefing. Another problem was that troops who would go on leave rarely followed any media. They were too preoccupied with their family problems, with gathering wood for the winter, providing for their children's education, dealing with domestic problems. These people had neither the interest nor the possibility to follow the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I ask one question in relation to one of the documents you have shown to the witness. You were shown this where you said it was just an instruction for prisoners of war, how to treat them. Now, that document explains that the ICRC could only speak with prisoner of war who would be prosecuted for war crimes or crimes against humanity in the presence of an examining magistrate or an investigative judge. What's the basis for this presence of such a judge under international law when the ICRC would visit such a prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't give you a reliable answer to this question because I see by the number here that this document was drafted in the legal section, but I know that a prisoner should be allowed to speak to representatives of the ICRC without the presence of anyone from the side who is holding these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But for certain situations, the document contradicts this. So if you have no explanation for that, we'll just move on. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can give you the position of the Defence. If somebody is submitted to the investigating judge, he is only -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- allow me to just be a bit amused. A minute ago where I asked for the position of the Defence you said I can't give it because you -- you should ask the witness. Now, I asked the witness something, and -- of factual about a document and what explains the content of the document. Now you say we can tell it what it is. We'll hear from you any submissions from that in the interpretation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can explain. The first one was factual question, the second one is legal question. And I come from that legal system, and I have a position on that one. On the matter of the signature of the gentleman where I was not present, I cannot have my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, my question was a factual one is whether this witness can explain the content of that. This witness can't do that. I take it that you will be in a position later to elaborate on it when you make any submissions on legal matters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 1D5422 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until we get some help from our colleague Mr. Traldi and Ms. Janet Stewart, we'll have to work with the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: We have looked at this document during proofing, the two of us. It's a document from the sector for intelligence and security affairs, the security administration, the Main Staff of the VRS. At the Main Staff, there was a security administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: At the Main Staff, was there an information administration?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: In para 2 in this document -- in fact, let's first read what it's about. The first paragraph says -- it's the first paragraph above what we see now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Bit more further -- up. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says in the middle of this paragraph: "As far as providing information to the public on combat activities from the 6th of October to the 12th of October 1995, it's necessary that security organs and units of military police fully comply with the cited orders." And there is an order from the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs of the Main Staff of the VRS cited at the top. In item 2, we read: "Individual reporters or crews from the media may enter the combat zone only with the approval of the Main Staff of the VRS, signed by the commander of the Main Staff, Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic or assistant commander Lieutenant-General Milan Gvero, or Colonel Savo Sokanovic, the head of the information administration." But you've just told us that there was no information administration at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you the chief of the information administration?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't be the chief of something that didn't exist. I wasn't, because there was no such administration. Second, I was head of the section for morale and religious affairs, not the section for information.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Even if we agree that the term is wrong, you were not chief of section for information either, were you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. Time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time for a break. And could you tell us how much -- Could first the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any forecast as far as timing is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will stay inside two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then before we take the break, I stopped you earlier when you wanted to explain on the basis of your knowledge of your own system. You may have misunderstood my question. My question was where the justification is found in international law. Because in the document, of course, it is easily stated that internal law would overrule Article 126 of the Geneva Convention of this -- on the treatment of prisoners of war, and that is -- we are looking forward if you, at a later point in time, deal with a legal issue how internal legislation could overrule any rights granted by the Geneva Conventions. We take a break, and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may move on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First I would tender 1D5422 to be MFI since we do not have translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's MFI D1058, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification pending uploading a translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask you about paramilitary formations. In the Main Staff, did you know that there were paramilitaries in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the Main Staff regarding members of the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The presence of paramilitaries was very pronounced at the beginning in the initial period. I don't want to go through all of their names, but I would like to say that the position of the Main Staff and the Army of Republika Srpska was that paramilitary units should be absolutely subordinated to the units of the VRS army, not just formally. Unfortunately, the process was very long and hard and despite the requests and demands of the political and military leaderships, some units that were subordinated to the VRS still acted as paramilitary formations and they were very hard to control and command. The last known presence of a paramilitary formation that I am aware of within the VRS was in 1995. I believe that it was in the month of October 1995. I'm talking about Arkan's unit. The commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, approached the president of Republika Srpska and gave him an ultimatum with regard to that unit, asking him that that unit should be removed from the territory of Republika Srpska, and that eventually happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness. When did the commander, General Mladic, approach the president? When did that take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When that paramilitary unit arrived in the western part of Republika Srpska. As far as I can remember, I believe that it was in the month of October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Banja Luka at the forward command post of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about the relationship with the civilian authorities. Did the military co-operate with the civilian authorities in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The military did co-operate with the civilian authorities. The quality of that co-operation ranged and it varied. Let me say that we co-operated with the local bodies of authority and economic entities, that co-operation with the brigade level. We co-operated with the regional authorities and economic structures, that co-operation was exercised by corps commands. And then at the level of the Main Staff, there was co-operation with the bodies of authority at the level of Republika Srpska, of course. Of course, there was no co-operation with the Supreme Command, who was the Supreme Commander, the military carried out his orders. But there was co-operation with the assembly, with the government, with commissions for refugees and displaced persons, with the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry for Religious Affairs, and all the other important organs of authorities that were of some significance for the functioning of defence and the military. That co-operation most commonly concerned the provision of bare necessities for the military, their families, and the families of fallen soldiers. The co-operation varied from one body to another. Among those who co-operated with the civilian authorities was also the Department for Information. That co-operation oscillated with time and it varied from one body to the other, so there were periods when there was very good co-operation with some bodies and then there was a lull in that co-operation or even a tension between those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any conflicts with any of the civilian authorities, especially when it came to the financial situation of the military?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were conflicts. One of the issues at stake was the concept of organising the military.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: What organ are you talking about, first of all.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence because the Ministry of Defence was in charge of providing finances for the military. The Ministry of Defence advocated a different way of organising the military. According to them, they wanted the logistics sector, the sector for organisation, personnel, and mobilisation, and the sector for morale guidance, religious affairs, and legal affairs to be parts of the Ministry of Defence, whereas the Main Staff would only have a commander and his staff. Also, there were conflicts with the Ministry of Information. There was also a period when -- or, rather, several periods when there were conflicts and tensions with the Supreme Commander, himself, i.e., the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at 1D5415. We'll check if we have a translation. It doesn't seem to have been uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you what the document is about. It was issued by the Main Staff of the VRS on the 26th January, 1994. It was faxed, and the signature block contains the name of Colonel Savo Sokanovic. Do you remember this document, Mr. Sokanovic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Under paragraph 1, it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we inquire whether any translation does exist? Is the Prosecution aware of -- Mr. Lukic, this is now the third document without a translation. Yes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I was just going to say no, we're not, and that we'd checked when we got the Defence's list whether we had translations for any of them and provided the ones we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, it cripples the Chamber, more or less, if we can't have a look at the document in its entirety and if you just read portions, and since this is now the third time today --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can -- since this is short document, if you want me, I can read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It takes more time, even. That's -- but let's -- if you first put your questions to the witness, then we'll ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sokanovic, the first thing that we can read in this document, apart from a list of addressees, including all the corps, as well as the air force and anti-aircraft defence, and some other units, it says here: "The government of Republika Srpska issued a decision on centralising all procurement for the VRS in 1994. Contracting procurements of equipment and materiel will be done by the Ministry of Defence. The military needs to express its requirements." In practice, did this decision ever take off the ground?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Now come that you issued this document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted after a session of the government of Republika Srpska. Numerous requests came from the VRS from its Main Staff to secure provisions for the military, and the government finally took it upon itself to arrange centralised procurement according to the requirements of the military. In that decision, it also says that requests should be submitted, segregated by the type of materiel and equipment and their quantities. On behalf of this sector, I sent this document to the units asking them to express their requirements and submit them to us so that they might be supplied with what they needed. Obviously, this refers to the requirements of the sector -- not only the sector but the entire organ for moral, guidance, religious and legal affairs across the board, across the military.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, how did your chain of procurement go? How did you get your supplies after January 1994? Did you continue sticking to your old ways or did the Ministry of Defence change its attitude towards the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing changed. Everything was as it had been before. As for my specific requirements, we did not receive anything. Everything was dealt with to the extent possible through the nations, through gifts from other bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
