utterances.text: This document is just an illustration of what you told us before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender it into evidence to be marked for identification first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1059.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. Next subject, please, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let me now ask you something about strategic goals. In your interview with the Prosecutor, you were asked about that. At the end of the war, did you have a very clear picture as to what the borders of Republika Srpska were or were to be?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up 1D5421.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you be a bit more precise by what you meant by "at the end of the war"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's how you understand the question as well, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we have another document without translation. We requested a translation but we haven't received it yet. This is a document issue by the sector for morale guidance, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, when did you request a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to check with my Case Manager. Probably not a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because if it was this morning or yesterday, then, of course, that sheds some light on level of preparation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It sheds lights more on our --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further comments, Mr. Lukic. I know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But if you comment on our work, we should probably have the right to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you're not in the same position as the Bench is. Let that be clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know, Mr. Sokanovic, how and why this document was created?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document was created after a session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska held in October 1995 after the fall of 30 municipalities in the western part of Republika Srpska and three municipalities in the area of Ozren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We - which I assume everyone understands not to mean me but Ms. Stewart - appear to have found a translation under a different ERN which we're going to pull up in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'd like to have a look at it. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: This document was shown to you by the Prosecution during your interview, if my notes are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we need page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Halfway through the page, we see: "The political leadership and the National Assembly have still not, to this day, determined the borders of Republika Srpska that the military are supposed to reach or to defend. Quite to the contrary. Most frequent discussions were about percentages and ceding territory." Who drafted this document, if you can remember, Mr. Sokanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can have maybe might try have English translation so you can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it's in Sanction, it may cause some problems, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I read everything I wanted from the B/C/S version, so we can have this section. It's last quarter of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could have the document on our screen through Sanction in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should start with: "... political leadership... "

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see you are on the signature line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have to go back, if you don't mind. Go back slowly. A bit further. A bit more. Yeah. A bit more. I didn't have this document, so I really couldn't locate where -- should be: "... the political leadership and assembly ..." A bit further up, please. Bit more. That's it, in the middle of the page. Thank you. "To this day, the political leadership and the National Assembly have not determined the borders of the RS which the army is supposed to defend or reach."

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of October, 1995, when this document was created -- in fact, from the 14th to the 16th October, when the 54th Session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska took place, combat had already been terminated and there was no more fighting until the signing of the Dayton Accords. Had you asked is the assembly or the government or the president before to tell you the objective of your fighting, all of it in the light of the strategic objectives that were put to you during the interview; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. I was asked about that during the interview and I said then that I personally, and many other people with whom I discussed it, did not know clearly defined objectives of the Army of Republika Srpska, and this gave rise to several letters addressed first to the Ministry of Defence, or the government, or the president of the republic - I can't remember anymore all the people to whom we wrote - asking that our goals be defined. Because all the time, as far as I know and the way I saw it, the objective we had in our head was to protect the population, to defend the territory, to restore peace that would be lasting and fair. That was the objective we had in our minds and the objective we pursued.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier today you gave us one example that, in your view, reflects that there were no objectives of the war, and you were talking about a village belonging to the other ethnic group situated very close to the Main Staff headquarters. Can you tell us the name of that village or those villages?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's Krivace Plane, Potplanje, Podzeplje. All of these villages were very close to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you were on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I don't recall the witness -- actually, if the witness could take off his head phones for a moment assuming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you speak or understand the English language, Witness? Could you take off your earphones for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I didn't re-call the witness's testimony -- I recalled the witness mentioning the example. I didn't recall his testimony, that this example reflected that there were no objectives of the war, and so I was wondering if Mr. Lukic could provide an explanation of -- or a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there was a spontaneous observation by the witness about protecting civilians in a nearby village, but Mr. Traldi is now asking about whether -- how to link that to the objectives of the war in the absence of such objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not on the record, it's still in my head. Maybe I jumped ahead because I know I spoke with this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and he mentioned that in this sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not as far as we could hear, but please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is speaking too loud -- too loudly and should refrain from doing that. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to inform my colleague that I'm closing to an end in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sokanovic, these villages you've just mentioned, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: There were armed people there. They had armed units. I don't think every resident had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know they were armed?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: We knew because on two occasions they had launched combat actions against members of the staff and staff units. In one incident, one person was killed, and in the other action, I believe 14 members of the VRS were captured.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it clear at that moment what should be done?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In that situation, the Army of Republika Srpska did not take any armed action. Instead, we tried to find a way towards peaceful co-existence.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: What part did you play in that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked on drafting a leaflet, a flyer with a proclamation that was to be addressed to the residents of these villages, saying that we should continue living peacefully side by side, that they should respect the authorities of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence to be MFI'd until the translation is verified, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, we saw thumbs up which you should refrain from doing. We heard again loud speaking. This is the last warning. The slightest contravention of what you are supposed to do will now immediately result in removal from the courtroom. Let that be clear. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you were on your feet. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Simply to say that we have no objection, and Ms. Stewart has provided the Defence's Case Manager with the translation, so I imagine it'll be uploaded and released shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. You have tendered the document when I intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's 1D -- or is it under different 65 ter -- no. It's 1D05421.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI D1060, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until we have the new translation attached to this one, we'll wait for a second to have it admitted and have it marked for identification until this administrative matter has been resolved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask you now briefly about your personal losses during the war. Did you lose anyone in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Who did you lose?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: My father.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: How did your father die?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: An armed unit of the so-called BH Army raided his unprotected village, torched the houses, looted the property, and killed those who had not managed to get away quickly enough. My father was an elderly man, ill. He didn't even have time to leave his house. He was torched together with the house. And I also lost another eight relatives, including two who had lived in Sarajevo and were identified rather late, in 2000-and-some year. They were identified at a location in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us exactly which location it was where they were exhumed.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Kazani.

utterances.speaker: MR.  LUKIC
utterances.text: General Sokanovic, thank you. This is all that we had for you at the moment. Thank you for answering our questions.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Sokanovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. You'll find Mr. Traldi to your right. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic mentioned your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor during direct examination. That was in 2004. Can I take it that your position is that you told the truth in that interview?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was a long interview, and communication wasn't very easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But your position is you told the truth; yes?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to briefly follow up on a couple of the topics that were discussed on direct examination. First, you mentioned that a state of war was not declared for the entire Republika Srpska. You're aware that a state of imminent threat of war had been declared beginning in April 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. At least I can't recall that at this moment. But the state of war was proclaimed towards the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall the Law on All People's Defence, the ONO?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the Law on All People's Defence of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall that under the law that one of the consequences of a declaration of a state of imminent threat of war is a general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not disputing that, but the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia no longer existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, a general mobilisation was declared in Republika Srpska, for instance, by President Karadzic on the 20th of May, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, an approximate date -- on that approximate date, the president of the republic issued the decision on the organisation and establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska and required the Main Staff to make a draft of that decision. So I suppose one of the things written there was that the units should be manned and they couldn't be manned without mobilisation. But the state of war was not declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall that under the ONO, one of the consequences of that general mobilisation was the transfer of the military to a wartime structure?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that and it doesn't sound logical, because if there's a state of war, then the army should be operating under wartime rules, and the state should be operating under wartime laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So you don't re-call Article 8 of the ONO clarifies that the armed forces and other state and other organs transfer from a peacetime form of organisation to a wartime form of organisation when mobilisation is introduced. Your testimony today is you don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I maintain that mobilisation in and of itself still does not mean a state of war. Because peacetime laws continue to be in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you weren't -- I have been asking about mobilisation. You weren't involved yourself in mobilisation or manning of the army; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, nor was I in the Army of Republika Srpska on that date in May. And even later, that is not within the competencies of the sector for morale, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You are familiar, however, with the combat readiness report that the army did, the VRS did in 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean analysis?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Of combat readiness for the VRS, yes.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not in detail but I know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would your sector have worked on the sections of the report dealing with, for instance, morale?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. That would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this is an authoritative document; yes?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to answer. I cannot assess its weight. It certainly has some weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, your sector and the other Main Staff sectors worked on analyses relevant to your own areas of work; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. And if we worked, because this is an analysis of the combat readiness of the army, we also gathered information from subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you gathered information from the corps, the corps gathered information from the brigades; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And this both reflected what the army had been doing and helped guide next steps; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, from theory, each analysis should involve dealing with one particular issue and end in a conclusion and a proposal of measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you wouldn't have worked on the section dealing with mobilisation and manning because that wasn't part of your responsibility; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we did not deal with that. But if it touched upon morale, it could have been mentioned as one of the factors impacting on the morale of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, but the mobilisation and manning sections would have been dealt with by the relevant Main Staff sector, not by your sector or your section; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the responsibility of the sector for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel, but the issue could also be treated in the part of the analysis that dealt with morale, religious, and legal affairs. It could be included there as an element that had a positive or adverse effect on the morale of the troops, on logistic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, since it could have an impact on morale, then you're surely aware that in the combat readiness report, the sector for organisation, mobilisation, and personal noted that three VRS corps - the SRK [Realtime transcript read in error "RSK"], the 1st Krajina Corps, and the Drina Corps - were actually manned above 100 per cent of the set manning levels; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, did you say RSK or SRK? You are recorded as RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's an important distinction and I did say SRK, I think. I certainly meant to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Would it be useful if I repeated the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's necessary. Certainly, all the elements were considered in some way to the extent needed. Whether that was taken into account at the time or not, I can't say. But I'm not challenging the facts you are putting to me or what is written there, but the quality of manning these corps and the entire army is very important. If you just allow me to say this --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Whether, for instance, we had enough officers and non-commissioned officers --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understand. What I'm asking you is, yes or no, whether you recall that as of the promulgation by the combat readiness report in the 1993, the three corps I mentioned - the Drina Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and the 1st Krajina Corps - were all manned in terms of number of personnel at above 100 per cent of establishment levels. Do you recall that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recall how establishment levels were set?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: For the entire military? Mr. Prosecutor, do you mean the entire military?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I mean do you recall how or who was responsible for determining what the establishment level of a particular brigade or a particular corps was.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that was established by the organs for organisation, mobilisation, and personnel affairs in consultation with organs at lower levels and in keeping with the prevalent rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, just quickly before we go to the break, you mentioned on direct that the corps commands and the air force command would include reports on morale in their daily combat reports. The commander of the Main Staff as well as the assistants to the commander had to be familiar with those daily combat reports; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that in regular combat reports at those levels of command, there was a paragraph referring to combat morale and situation on the front line. This doesn't mean that all assistant commanders were familiar with those reports. If all of them were present, which was rare, I can't rule out the fact that they may have been informed. However, it would be the chief of sector for morale, religious, and personnel affairs or legal affairs who would be best suited to learn about that particular paragraph in combat reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you said before we go to the break. That was three minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I see we're now at the time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break. Witness, you may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just if I might use the time, if we could pull up 65 ter 07988.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, this is the 1st Krajina Corps' report dated the 30th of September, 1992, on current issues of combat morale. This is a document that, based on your position at the time, you would have reviewed personally; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I was still not the chief of department for moral guidance and religious affairs. Dosen Zivko was still in that position. This doesn't mean that I did not review the document, but I would need some time to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's look at page 2 for the moment in both languages, and I'm interested in the second paragraph in both languages. The 1st Krajina Corps is writing about UNPROFOR, the Red Cross, and then in the second paragraph refers to certain journalists who they suggest are writing more and more objectively and portraying the real state of affairs and give a certain confidence and belief in their good intentions. They say: "Soldiers and units have accepted with trust only the Russian delegation and the most recent articles in the Russian press." Now, it's clear that the 1st Krajina Corps' organ for legal, moral, and religious affairs was able to keep track of what was going on in the international press; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose so because they were in a big city, and it was the strongest information department with a well-developed press centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, as one of the officers in that department, Milos Solaja testified they had an analytical group for monitoring international media; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Quite possible yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you told Mr. Lukic on direct examination that you weren't able to keep track of what going on in the international press. In fact, the Main Staff could simply have asked one of its subordinate corps; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Hmm, they could but they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, among other things, they were receiving information in these morale reports on what the international press was saying, weren't they? Like we see here.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were just sporadic examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when international media coverage was published either on Bosnian Serb television, or the Bosnian Serb press, the press in the Republic of Serbia, or the press in Croatia, or in Bosnian territory, the Main Staff's sector for legal, moral, and religious affairs would track it through its monitoring of those sources of media; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you that neither the sector nor the information department that were in charge of this had no technical capabilities for direct monitoring. They also couldn't read foreign press. The only newspapers that they could read were those from Republika Srpska and Serbia. They knew as much as they could hear or read in the domestic media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in fact, your -- the instruction you drafted that General Mladic signed that Mr. Lukic showed you on direct - and for the record, that's P5082 - that talks about monitoring enemy media, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the instruction was drafted in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, when you were asked about it in your interview, you said this department had a duty to -- first to watch Muslim and Croat TV stations so that -- to see what kind of information they are broadcasting. Do you stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by that, with a caveat: I don't recall having mentioned Croatian media, but I'm not excluding that. I don't remember having mentioned TV situations but, rather, radio stations. We could not receive any television signals that didn't emanate from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it -- is it well understood yet in your interview you did not mention TV and only radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, that's correct. They could monitor radio and television programmes of Republika Srpska and those of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said they could monitor radio and television programmes. And a minute ago, you said: "We could not receive any television signals that didn't emanate from Republika Srpska." So you're excluding Croatian television; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember, and based on what I can remember, I would exclude that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Traldi, I don't know whether -- I take it that there's a verbatim transcript of the interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there is an audio recording?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please read to the witness then what he said if you did not yet intend to do that. Witness, we have an audio recording -- well, the Chamber not yet, but there is an audio recording of your interview. So therefore, if you are telling us that the transcript is not accurate - and Mr. Traldi will put it to you most likely - then we'll just check it on the basis of the audio to find out whether you said -- referred to television in that context or not. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 32563. And we'll be looking for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: While it comes up, if I might tender the last document, just so I don't forget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 07988 will be Exhibit P7390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7390 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could have page 44 in the English and 55 in the B/C/S. And, I'm sorry, I'm seeing a different page in the B/C/S than I'd expected. If we could have e-court page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the English? And for B/C/S -- it comes in the reversed sequence. Usually we have the B/C/S at the left and ... I do not mind, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am afraid I do, as we're not -- we now don't have the right page. If we could have 44 in the English and 55 in the B/C/S. And the English, it will be listed as the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have two times the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we see starting at the bottom of the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we don't have the right page in B/C/S yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I apologise. And if we could go back, I think, a single page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have -- I don't know whether the page numbering at the bottom corresponds with the page numbers. It seems at least in the English that it does, but it looks as if we are on page 14 now on the B/C/S, which is difficult to understand as corresponding with page 55 unless there are more documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My understanding is the B/C/S pages are numbered by the tape, whereas the English is numbered as a whole. And we can see on the English we're looking for the start of T000-2724A. And it appears to me the start of that is on page 55 in the B/C/S. Now, we see at the very bottom of the English that the interviewer refers to a paragraph in the document dealing with the monitoring of enemy media, and if we could then turn to the next page in both languages. Now, we have -- sorry. If we could go back to the bottom of the previous page in the B/C/S. I'd skipped an important portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see you describe, beginning at line 20, the duty of the information department regarding the monitoring of enemy media. Is it clear to you from what's written there that this included monitoring Muslim and Croat television, based on your answer in your interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where do we see this in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is clear -- if the witness can take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please take off your headphones for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is clear translation issue. It says "stations." In English we have TV stations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- what exactly are we talking about? Lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Line 20 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Line 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in B/C/S. Line 2 in English. And then in line 23 in B/C/S, it says what is not TV. In English we have TV added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could perhaps the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To read --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, Witness, could you put on your earphones again. Could you slowly read what is recorded here as -- on line 20, can you read that? Where it starts with: "Ovi organi..." Could you slowly read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "These organs therefore monitor the media of the enemy, the opponent, and our own information about the enemy published in the media. Namely this organ, i.e., the department that was in charge to the extent possible, monitor Muslim and Croatian stations and to listen to what they publish and to monitor stations of Republika Srpska and to see what they publish."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now I heard the witness read quite a bit in the beginning of what something that doesn't appear at all in the English. Or am I wrong? It's certainly not the same -- well, I think it is -- what then follows seems to be more or less the same, that is, about radio and newspapers and then the confirmation by the witness, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in Serbian it's "listen" in English it says "watch."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this portion certainly needs -- Witness, you will understand that we carefully look at what your statement is and -- Mr. Traldi, it may be that you move on for the time being and that you have it reviewed so that we can be certain that what is put to the witness is really what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll certainly do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do, Mr. Traldi. Did I hear you correct that you said the English is the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, and it -- well, it's been uploaded as the original but it's based on an audio recorded interview where the witness would have been speaking in Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So it's actually in terms of the audio Serbian is the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. And the audio is what we'll check against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But here a technique is used in which one portion is in the one language and -- one version is the one language, the other one in the other language, whereas sometimes we have a different technique being used for recording; that is, that always the switch from one language to the other can be followed on the one and only transcript. Here, apparently, work has been done on it, and I take it that we would consider whatever is spoken in English in that respect as original, and whatever is spoken in B/C/S, that in that respect it is original. That's how I understand the technique being used here. So if you verify it, then it should be done on the basis of the audio checking whether B/C/S-spoken words appear right in the B/C/S. And then later, of course, the translations become relevant as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have a bit to do or to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll try to handle it, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to turn to a different topic. One of the things that your Main Staff sector did was publish a magazine called Srpska Vojska; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 02362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: 02362. And in line 10 I think I'd said they published the magazine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is the transcript of the 22nd Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly held on the 23rd and 24th of November, 1992. This is around the time Srpska Vojska was created; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, in fact, you and General Gvero went to the assembly to attend a promotion for the first issue; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably. Although I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 29 in the English and page 28 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see a reference to the promotion of the magazine. We read a reference to Minister Ostojic speaking. He was the minister for information in the RS government at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now he says in pertinent part beginning in the fourth line and in reference to Srpska Vojska: "The very name and emblem of the magazine, which is issued by the editorial office of the Main Staff of the Serbian army, shows that the news network ... of the Serbian people is developing in the direction determined by the SDS, and carried out and channelled by the National Assembly and its executive organs." He's describing here the role and function of Srpska Vojska; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he, indeed, describes that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now below that - and turning to the next page in the B/C/S - we see your superior, General Gvero speak. And in the second paragraph of his remarks, he says, in pertinent part, that Srpska Vojska has a small editorial board and "it is my pleasure to present to you Lieutenant-Colonel Savo Sokanovic, a young editor and a local man." Now this is a reference to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Although I haven't found it in the text, but I believe what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, in the B/C/S version, it's under General Gvero's name, in the second full paragraph, the fifth line on the far right. Do you see it? I see you've nodded but you have to articulate your answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: I found it. Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Second-Lieutenant Djurdjevic he refers, who he says is the editor, that's also an officer in the Main Staff's sector for legal, morale, and religious affairs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that time he was head of the section for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, P7196 consists of an excerpt from this assembly session. What I'd request leave to do is simply add these pages in both languages to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if there's anything for contextualisation you would like to add, I take it that you'll inform Mr. Traldi without delay. We'll wait and see how the extract is changed and then an instruction will be given to Mr. Registrar once you have uploaded the new extract. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now can we have 65 ter 19225.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What we see here is the first issue of Srpska Vojska dated the 18th of November, 1992. Now turning to page 2 in both languages, we see an editorial by General Gvero titled: "The Voice of Serbian Dignity and Chivalry." Turning to page 3 in the middle in the English and towards the bottom of the page in the B/C/S, the eighth paragraph, so the third paragraph from the bottom, we see that he writes in pertinent part: "Our greatest value is the unity of the political and military leadership at all levels of the state, the unity of the people and the army, and a willingness to fight for victory." General Gvero is setting out the state of co-operation between the VRS and the political authorities at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is a feature from this magazine from the very beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and his message is, if I have the right to interpret someone else's words at all, is what our greatest value is, and I personally don't see anything wrong with it. Unity of the political --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- leadership, the army, and the people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- no one is claiming that there is anything wrong in it. Mr. Traldi just seeks your confirmation of this being an expression of the co-operation between the civilian structures and the military structures. You are -- apparently you have something on your mind that you are accused of something, which is not the case. You appear as a witness. So I do understand that you say there's nothing wrong, but it does express as was suggested by Mr. Traldi ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just say briefly one thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if it's relevant, as in to the answer, then we'd like to hear it, otherwise ... otherwise not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that this is the beginning, the early days of the fighting, December 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's the reason why Mr. Traldi mentioned the date: November 1990 -- I think it was November 1992 instead of December 1991, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're referring to December 1991, Witness, but the document we looked at is the first edition which was published in November 1992. You agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just so the record is clear, I take it you agree that General Gvero is there setting out the state of co-operation between the military and civilian authorities as of November 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, reading this text it appears to be so, but this can also be interpreted as something that would be desirable. We need this unity. It's our greatest value. That's the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now some of the other things we read in this text are references to a 500-year Turkish occupation, reference to forced conversions of Serbs, and a description of the war to that point as a "national liberation war to save and preserve the Serbian people." Past crimes against Serbs and the need to preserve the very existence of the Serbian people by winning the war were ongoing themes in Srpska Vojska's work; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: In our lands, it's very difficult to get a view of anything without looking back to the past. Regrettably so. And unfortunately some of the causes of this conflict lie in the unresolved matters from before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the question was a different one: Whether past crimes against Serbs and the need to preserve the very existence of the Serbian people by winning the war, whether these were ongoing themes in Srpska Vojska's work. Were they or were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were themes, but certainly not ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning briefly to page 4 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S, and I see the time, so I'm going to ask you just three very focused questions about this article. This is an interview with General Mladic titled: "Our Enemies Have No Chance." He is asked at first about the struggle so far and refers to avoiding what he calls a new 1941. This is also a reference to past crimes against Serbs; correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Later in his answer at the end of the first column in the B/C/S, we see that he says that: "At all events we should thank all those progressive people and the movement or, rather, the SDS who woke the bulk of the Serbian people and opened their eyes to these stormy events, which undoubtedly saved many of them." This is an illustration of the unity General Gvero was describing between the military and political leadership at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And at that time, there were no great differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 7 in the English, page 5 in the B/C/S in the middle, we read General Mladic is asked about differences between the VRS and the JNA, and he says, in pertinent part: "The difference between our army and the JNA is that this is an army with a clear goal before it." At that point, the objectives of the war, the six strategic objectives, were perfectly clear to General Mladic and to the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Is it read to the witness or is General Mladic referencing so those six objectives? Can we find it in the text?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's -- well, I didn't understand the question to be that it quoted literally General Mladic. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's correct. What I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps you rephrase the question in such a way that Mr. Lukic's concerns are removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll break it up into two very short yes or no questions, sir. General Mladic says: "The difference between our army and the former JNA is that this is an army with a clear goal before it." Now, that reflects that at that point General Mladic and the VRS were clear about the goals of the war; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for speculation. What General Mladic thought at that time, this witness cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The witness testified he was one of the editors of this publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Editor? [Indiscernible] everything what somebody thinks or means? Could he project to publish something? It's very broad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was broader than just General Mladic. You as an editor of this publication and as a member of the VRS, do you understand this to be an expression that the objectives of the war were clear for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The letters are very small. Could you please highlight this passage for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the relevant portion be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We are looking for the third column, I believe, in the B/C/S at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think we cannot continue this way today. We should read everything what General Mladic said what the objective is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can do so in re-examination. The questions are now focusing on what is published here as an interview, or at least that's how I understand what it is, an interview in this magazine with General Mladic. And if there are good reasons to believe that this is not what he said, you have an opportunity in re-examination, Mr. Lukic, to address that matter. Witness, is it large enough for you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see the text, but I don't see any "goals."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, the question was plural. Here we have one goal. So it's misleading as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- have you found where it says what -- that this is an army with a ... let me just see. You read the relevant portion, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now Srpska Vojska quotes General Mladic saying the difference between our army and the former JNA is that this is an army with a clear goal before it. Now, first, you understand that to mean that the purpose of the war was clear at that time, right, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, he is speaking in the same sense that I mentioned before that it was -- the goal was the protection of the people, the defence of the territory, the restoration of peace --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I hadn't asked you at this stage yet what the goal was. What he is saying -- what you understand him to be saying is that the purpose of the war at that stage is clear. Yes?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SOKANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. I'll explore the topic further tomorrow. I'd ask that a number be reserved for these three articles from this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you already reserve a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P7391, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Witness, we'd like to see you back tomorrow at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom. But before you leave this courtroom, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, irrespective of whether that is testimony you have given today or whether it is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, which three articles are you talking about? Are you talking about the three --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd -- what I'd meant was, and I spoke, I think, imprecisely, the cover, General Gvero's piece, and then the interview with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 19225.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: From 19225, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, when you earlier said that you had not asked yet what these goals or that goal would be, you may have forgotten about that you, in page 76, line 4, you said: "At that point the objectives of the war, the six strategic objectives were perfectly clear to General Mladic." So you did clearly refer to what a goal or the goals would have been and therefore it was not fair to the witness to say I didn't ask you that yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. I'd simply intended to focus the witness on the immediately preceding question and I -- of course, I did so inartfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but he could have been confused and could have thought that you were still thinking in terms of the six strategic goals. We -- with apologies, we were unable to finish on time. We'll adjourn for the day and we resume tomorrow, 19th of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of May, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.25 p.m.,
